prompt: An unresponsive adult with no suspected trauma has gurgling respirations and vomitus in the mouth. What is your first airway action?

options.text: Roll onto the side, suction, then reassess breathing
Insert an oropharyngeal airway, then suction around it
Give two rescue breaths by pocket mask, then suction
Keep the patient supine and perform a head-tilt chin-lift

explanation: Gurgling means fluid is sitting in the upper airway. Rolling the patient onto the side lets vomitus drain and suctioning the oropharynx clears the rest; adjuncts and ventilations come only after the airway is clear, followed by reassessment of breathing.

distractorExplanations.b: An OPA placed over vomitus can push material deeper; clear the airway with suction before inserting any adjunct.
distractorExplanations.c: Ventilating before clearing vomitus forces it into the lungs; suction first, then ventilate only if breathing is inadequate.
distractorExplanations.d: Supine positioning lets vomitus pool in the airway; the patient is rolled to the side so fluids drain and suction can clear them.

prompt: Which patient is the best candidate for a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)?

options.text: Unresponsive patient with severe facial fractures after an assault
Drowsy patient with a clenched jaw and an intact gag reflex
Alert patient speaking in full sentences with a mild wheeze
Unresponsive patient with no gag reflex and a clear midface

explanation: An NPA is tolerated by patients who still have a gag reflex or a clenched jaw, where an OPA would cause gagging or cannot be inserted. It keeps the tongue off the back of the pharynx in a semiconscious patient who needs help maintaining the airway.

distractorExplanations.a: Severe facial or suspected basilar skull fractures contraindicate an NPA because the tube may pass into the cranial vault or damaged tissue.
distractorExplanations.c: A patient talking in full sentences is maintaining the airway; an adjunct adds discomfort without benefit.
distractorExplanations.d: With no gag reflex and an intact face, an oropharyngeal airway is the usual first adjunct; the NPA's advantage is tolerance with a gag reflex.

prompt: In which situation should you avoid the head-tilt chin-lift and open the airway with a jaw-thrust instead?

options.text: An unresponsive asthma patient with severe wheezing
An unresponsive patient with loose dentures in the mouth
An unresponsive patient found at the bottom of a ladder
An unresponsive patient who still has a gag reflex

explanation: A fall from a ladder is a mechanism for cervical spine injury. Tilting the head extends the neck, so the jaw-thrust with manual inline stabilization is used instead; if the jaw-thrust fails to open the airway, airway takes priority per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Asthma narrows the lower airways and does not change how the upper airway is opened; head-tilt chin-lift is fine without trauma.
distractorExplanations.b: Loose dentures are removed before ventilation, but they do not make the head-tilt chin-lift contraindicated.
distractorExplanations.d: A present gag reflex rules out an oropharyngeal airway, not the manual head-tilt chin-lift maneuver.

prompt: A conscious adult is choking, cannot speak, and has an ineffective cough. What should you do?

options.text: Encourage forceful coughing and monitor closely
Give 5 back blows, then 5 chest thrusts as for an infant
Perform a blind finger sweep to remove the object
Give abdominal thrusts until obstruction clears

explanation: Complete airway obstruction in a conscious adult warrants abdominal thrusts per AHA BLS. Continue until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unresponsive, then begin CPR.

distractorExplanations.a: Coughing is encouraged only when the cough is effective; a silent, ineffective cough means severe obstruction needing thrusts.
distractorExplanations.b: Back blows alternating with chest thrusts is the infant sequence; a conscious choking adult receives abdominal thrusts.
distractorExplanations.c: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only an object you can see, and use abdominal thrusts first.

prompt: You are ventilating an apneic adult who has a pulse with a bag-valve-mask (BVM). Which finding best shows that each breath is adequate?

options.text: Visible chest rise over about 1 second per breath
Abdominal rise with each squeeze of the bag
Breaths delivered at 30 per minute to raise SpO2 quickly
An SpO2 rise within the first 10 seconds of bagging

explanation: Each breath is delivered over about 1 second with just enough volume to make the chest visibly rise. For an adult with a pulse, current AHA guidance is about 1 breath every 6 seconds (10 per minute); extra volume or rate only inflates the stomach.

distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal rise means air is entering the stomach from excess volume or poor head position, not effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty breaths per minute is hyperventilation; it causes gastric inflation and reduces venous return and cardiac output.
distractorExplanations.d: Pulse oximetry lags behind changes in ventilation; visible chest rise is the immediate bedside indicator.

prompt: You are choosing an oropharyngeal airway (OPA) for an unresponsive adult with no gag reflex. How do you measure the correct size?

options.text: Tip of the nose to the earlobe on the same side
Corner of the mouth to the angle of the mandible
Bridge of the nose to the cleft of the chin
Width of the patient's little finger

explanation: An OPA is sized from the corner of the mouth to the angle of the jaw (some texts use the earlobe). A device that is too long can fold the epiglottis over the glottis; one that is too short pushes the tongue back into the airway.

distractorExplanations.a: Nose-tip-to-earlobe is the sizing method for a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA), not an oropharyngeal airway.
distractorExplanations.c: Bridge of nose to chin cleft is how a BVM or pocket mask is sized, not the length of an OPA.
distractorExplanations.d: Little-finger width is a rough guide to nasopharyngeal airway diameter; an OPA's length is measured from mouth corner to jaw angle.

prompt: You are ventilating a patient with a BVM, but resistance is high and the chest barely rises. What should you do first?

options.text: Squeeze the bag harder to overcome the resistance
Switch to a nonrebreather mask at 15 L/min
Reposition the head/jaw and confirm a mask seal
Begin abdominal thrusts for a foreign-body airway

explanation: Poor chest rise is most often caused by a leaking mask seal or an incompletely opened airway. Reposition the head and jaw, reseal the mask (two-person technique if possible), and retry before assuming a foreign-body obstruction.

distractorExplanations.a: More force increases gastric inflation without fixing the cause; poor chest rise usually means poor position or seal.
distractorExplanations.b: A nonrebreather does not ventilate; a patient who needs BVM support still needs positive-pressure breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: Thrusts are for obstruction that persists after the airway is repositioned; reposition and check the seal first.

prompt: A diner is coughing forcefully after a piece of food went down the wrong way. He can speak and is moving air well. What should you do?

options.text: Give abdominal thrusts until he stops coughing
Give five back blows between the shoulder blades
Encourage him to keep coughing and stay with him
Perform a finger sweep to look for the food

explanation: A patient who can speak and cough forcefully has a mild (partial) obstruction with good air exchange; his own cough is the most effective way to clear it. Stay with him, encourage coughing, and act with thrusts only if the cough becomes weak or silent or he cannot speak.

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal thrusts are for severe obstruction (cannot speak, silent or weak cough); they are not used while a strong cough is moving air.
distractorExplanations.b: Back blows are part of infant choking care and are not used on an adult who is still coughing forcefully and speaking.
distractorExplanations.d: Finger sweeps risk pushing the food deeper and are done only to remove an object you can actually see in an unresponsive patient.

prompt: A motorcyclist thrown from his bike is unresponsive with snoring respirations. Which technique should you use to open his airway?

options.text: Jaw-thrust while maintaining manual inline stabilization
Head-tilt chin-lift with a cervical collar applied
Modified chin-lift with the head turned to one side
Nasopharyngeal airway insertion before any manual maneuver

explanation: When spinal injury is suspected, the jaw-thrust lifts the tongue off the airway by moving the mandible forward without tilting the head, while the head is held in line. If the jaw-thrust cannot open the airway, the airway takes priority per protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Head-tilt chin-lift extends the neck even with a collar in place; jaw-thrust with manual stabilization is used instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Turning the head rotates the cervical spine; the head is held neutral and inline while the jaw is thrust forward.
distractorExplanations.d: An adjunct comes after the airway is opened manually, and NPAs are avoided with suspected facial or basilar skull fractures.

prompt: A COPD patient on a nonrebreather at 15 L/min becomes sleepy, with shallow respirations at 8 per minute. What should the EMR do?

options.text: Keep the nonrebreather unchanged and recheck in 15 minutes
Assist ventilations with a BVM connected to oxygen
Turn off the oxygen so the hypoxic drive can recover
Switch to a nasal cannula at 2 L/min and observe

explanation: Sleepiness with slow, shallow breathing means ventilation is now inadequate. The fix is positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM and oxygen, not withdrawing oxygen; once breathing is supported, oxygen is titrated to the protocol target for COPD.

distractorExplanations.a: Leaving a nonrebreather in place ignores that breathing is now inadequate; a mask cannot move air for a patient who is hypoventilating.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypoxia kills faster than carbon dioxide retention; oxygen is titrated per protocol, never withdrawn from a patient who needs it.
distractorExplanations.d: Lowering the flow does nothing for shallow, slow breathing; inadequate ventilation needs positive-pressure breaths, not a lower FiO2.

prompt: You are suctioning vomitus from an unresponsive adult's oropharynx. How long should each suction attempt last?

options.text: No more than 5 seconds, with no reoxygenation needed
No more than 15 seconds, reoxygenating between attempts
Up to 30 seconds per pass for thick secretions
Continuously until the airway is completely clear

explanation: Suction removes oxygen along with fluid, so each adult attempt is limited to about 15 seconds (children about 10, infants about 5). Ventilate or oxygenate between attempts; if vomitus keeps coming, roll the patient and alternate suction with ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Five seconds is the infant limit, and every pass removes oxygen, so reoxygenation between attempts is still needed.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty-second passes cause hypoxia; for thick secretions, use repeated brief passes alternating with ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Continuous suction causes hypoxia and vagal bradycardia; suction in brief passes with reoxygenation in between.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local short-stem expansion

prompt: A patient in severe respiratory distress who is breathing adequately needs the highest oxygen concentration you can give without ventilating. Which device delivers it when fitted properly?

options.text: Nasal cannula at 6 L/min, its maximum flow
Simple face mask at 10 L/min without a reservoir bag
Venturi mask set to a 40% oxygen concentration
Nonrebreather mask with reservoir at adequate flow

explanation: A nonrebreather with an inflated reservoir and a good seal, run at 10-15 L/min (enough to keep the bag from collapsing on inhalation), delivers roughly 90% oxygen, the highest of the non-ventilating devices an EMR uses.

distractorExplanations.a: A nasal cannula at 6 L/min delivers only about 44% oxygen, far below a nonrebreather with reservoir.
distractorExplanations.b: A simple mask tops out around 40–60%; without a reservoir bag it cannot match a nonrebreather's concentration.
distractorExplanations.c: A Venturi delivers precise low-to-moderate fixed concentrations (about 24–50%), below a nonrebreather.

prompt: After successful defibrillation, an adult has a palpable pulse (ROSC) but is still not breathing. What care does the patient need?

options.text: Oxygen and ventilatory support per protocol
Nonrebreather oxygen at 15 L/min without ventilations
Chest compressions resumed at 100–120 per minute
Rapid ventilation at 30 breaths/min to clear CO2

explanation: ROSC restores circulation, not necessarily breathing. An apneic patient with a pulse needs positive-pressure ventilation with supplemental oxygen at about 1 breath every 6 seconds, titrated per protocol, plus frequent pulse checks and pulse oximetry.

distractorExplanations.b: An apneic patient cannot draw in nonrebreather oxygen; apnea after ROSC still requires positive-pressure ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: ROSC means a pulse is present; compressions resume only if the pulse is lost again.
distractorExplanations.d: Hyperventilation after ROSC lowers cardiac output and cerebral blood flow; ventilate about 10 times per minute.

prompt: You are giving rescue breaths through a pocket mask with a one-way valve. How should each breath be delivered?

options.text: Deliver large, forceful breaths to overcome the valve
Deliver breaths over 1 second watching for chest rise
Remove the one-way valve to deliver more air volume
Seal the mask over the mouth only, leaving the nose open

explanation: Pocket mask breaths follow the same AHA rule as other rescue breaths: about 1 second each, with just enough volume to make the chest rise. The mask seals over both mouth and nose, and the one-way valve protects the rescuer.

distractorExplanations.a: The one-way valve adds little resistance; forceful breaths inflate the stomach and raise the risk of vomiting.
distractorExplanations.c: The valve protects the rescuer from exhaled air and fluids; removing it adds infection risk without improving ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: The pocket mask covers both mouth and nose; leaving the nose open lets air escape and causes poor chest rise.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: During an anaphylactic reaction, which findings indicate that upper airway swelling is getting worse?

options.text: Expiratory wheezing with a prolonged exhalation phase
Hives spreading across the chest, back, and arms
Progressive stridor, drooling, and difficulty swallowing
Crackles at both lung bases with pink, frothy sputum production

explanation: Swelling of the tongue, larynx, and throat narrows the upper airway: stridor that becomes louder or constant, drooling, and trouble swallowing mean obstruction may soon be complete. Give epinephrine per protocol, prepare to manage the airway, and transport immediately.

distractorExplanations.a: Wheezing reflects lower airway bronchospasm; upper airway swelling shows inspiratory stridor and voice change.
distractorExplanations.b: Spreading hives show skin involvement of the allergic reaction, not narrowing of the upper airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Crackles and frothy sputum suggest pulmonary edema in the alveoli, not swelling of the upper airway.

sourceNote: Original UniPrep2Go local bank (Wave 4). · Local QA repair (stems/distractors)

prompt: A 6-month-old has a pulse of 110 but is not breathing. At what rate do you give rescue breaths?

options.text: About 8-10 breaths per minute
About 10-12 breaths per minute
About 20-30 breaths per minute
About 40-60 breaths per minute

explanation: Current AHA guidance for an infant or child with a pulse but inadequate breathing is 1 breath every 2-3 seconds, about 20-30 breaths per minute, each over about 1 second with visible chest rise. Reassess the pulse about every 2 minutes.

distractorExplanations.a: Eight to ten per minute is below even the adult rate; infants need faster breaths to match their higher metabolic demand.
distractorExplanations.b: Ten to twelve per minute approximates the adult rate (1 breath every 6 seconds), too slow for an infant with a pulse.
distractorExplanations.d: Forty to sixty per minute is hyperventilation that causes gastric inflation and reduces venous return in an infant.

prompt: You are about to place a nonrebreather mask on a patient in respiratory distress. What must you do before putting the mask on the face?

options.text: Fill the reservoir bag by covering the valve with a finger
Set the flow to 2 L/min so the patient can adjust to it
Remove the one-way valves so the patient can inhale easily
Connect the mask to a humidifier filled with tap water

explanation: The reservoir must be pre-filled with oxygen (cover the valve until the bag inflates) and the flow set high enough, usually 10-15 L/min, to keep the bag from collapsing on inhalation. An empty reservoir leaves the patient breathing through a nearly sealed mask.

distractorExplanations.b: Two liters per minute cannot keep the reservoir inflated; the patient would rebreathe carbon dioxide and suffocate under the mask.
distractorExplanations.c: The one-way valves keep exhaled air out of the reservoir and room air out of the mask; removing them lowers the oxygen delivered.
distractorExplanations.d: Humidification is optional for long transports and uses sterile water; it is not the required step before applying the mask.

prompt: A calm adult at rest is breathing regularly with good chest rise. Which respiratory rate falls within the normal adult range?

options.text: 8 breaths per minute
16 breaths per minute
28 breaths per minute
36 breaths per minute

explanation: The normal resting respiratory rate for an adult is about 12-20 breaths per minute, with regular rhythm and adequate depth. Rates outside that range, or a normal rate with shallow depth, should prompt assessment of breathing adequacy.

distractorExplanations.a: Eight per minute is bradypnea in an adult and may signal respiratory depression, such as from opioids or head injury.
distractorExplanations.c: Twenty-eight per minute is tachypnea in an adult and suggests distress, fever, pain, or compensation for shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty-six per minute is markedly fast for an adult at rest and points to significant respiratory distress.

prompt: A 2-year-old with croup has been working hard to breathe for hours. Which finding indicates the child is tiring and may need ventilatory support?

options.text: A loud, barking cough with each crying spell
Vigorous crying when separated from a parent
A respiratory rate of 34 while alert and fussy
A slowing respiratory rate with drowsiness

explanation: Children compensate for respiratory distress until they tire. A falling respiratory rate combined with decreasing responsiveness signals impending respiratory failure, not improvement, and calls for assisted ventilation and rapid transport.

distractorExplanations.a: A barking cough is the hallmark of croup and shows the child is still moving air forcefully; it is not a sign of fatigue.
distractorExplanations.b: Vigorous crying means good energy and air movement; a child in respiratory failure becomes quiet and listless.
distractorExplanations.c: A rate in the 30s with alertness is within or near the toddler range and shows the child is still compensating.

prompt: A choking adult you were giving abdominal thrusts to becomes unresponsive. After lowering him to the floor and calling for help, what should you do next?

options.text: Begin CPR, looking in the mouth before giving breaths
Continue abdominal thrusts with the patient lying supine
Perform blind finger sweeps until the object is found
Give rescue breaths only until the chest finally rises

explanation: When a choking adult becomes unresponsive, begin CPR starting with chest compressions. Each time you open the airway to give breaths, look in the mouth and remove an object only if you can see it, then continue compressions.

distractorExplanations.b: Once the patient is unresponsive, chest compressions replace abdominal thrusts because they generate higher airway pressure and circulate blood.
distractorExplanations.c: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper; remove only an object you can see when you open the mouth.
distractorExplanations.d: Breaths alone neither expel the object nor circulate blood; an unresponsive choking patient needs full CPR starting with compressions.

prompt: A conscious woman in late pregnancy is choking and cannot speak. Which technique should you use?

options.text: Abdominal thrusts just above the navel, as for other adults
Back blows alone until the object dislodges
Chest thrusts on the center of the breastbone
A blind finger sweep, then abdominal thrusts

explanation: For choking patients in late pregnancy or who are too large to encircle at the abdomen, the rescuer gives chest thrusts on the lower half of the breastbone instead of abdominal thrusts, repeating until the object is expelled or the patient becomes unresponsive.

distractorExplanations.a: Abdominal thrusts in late pregnancy compress the uterus and are ineffective because the rescuer cannot reach around the abdomen properly.
distractorExplanations.b: Back blows alone are the infant sequence component; a conscious choking adult needs thrusts that raise airway pressure.
distractorExplanations.d: Blind finger sweeps can push the object deeper and are never the first step for a conscious choking patient.

prompt: A patient who had a laryngectomy and breathes through a neck stoma is apneic with a pulse. How should you deliver ventilations?

options.text: Seal a BVM mask over the mouth and nose as usual
Cover the stoma and ventilate through the mouth
Insert an OPA, then ventilate through the mouth
Seal a small BVM mask directly over the stoma

explanation: A laryngectomy patient breathes through the stoma, so ventilations go through it: use an infant or child mask sealed over the stoma and watch for chest rise. If air escapes from the mouth or nose (partial laryngectomy), seal them.

distractorExplanations.a: After a total laryngectomy, the mouth and nose no longer connect to the lungs, so mouth-and-nose ventilation moves no air.
distractorExplanations.b: Covering the stoma blocks the only airway; in a total laryngectomy patient the mouth does not lead to the trachea.
distractorExplanations.c: An OPA keeps the tongue off the pharynx, but the pharynx no longer connects to the trachea in a laryngectomy patient.

prompt: You are inserting a nasopharyngeal airway into a patient's right nostril. How should the device be prepared and positioned?

options.text: Water-soluble lubricant, with the bevel toward the septum
Petroleum jelly, with the bevel toward the outer nostril
No lubricant, inserted upside down and rotated 180 degrees
Water-soluble lubricant, aimed upward toward the eye

explanation: Lubricate the NPA with a water-soluble lubricant, insert it in the larger nostril (usually the right) with the bevel facing the septum, and advance it gently straight back along the floor of the nasal cavity until the flange rests on the nostril.

distractorExplanations.b: Petroleum-based lubricant can damage tissue and is not used; the bevel faces the septum, not the outer wall.
distractorExplanations.c: Inserting upside down and rotating 180 degrees is the adult OPA technique, and an unlubricated NPA injures the nasal mucosa.
distractorExplanations.d: The NPA is advanced straight back along the floor of the nose, not upward, which would strike the turbinates and cause bleeding.

prompt: How should an oropharyngeal airway be inserted in an unresponsive 4-year-old with no gag reflex?

options.text: Upside down along the palate, then rotated 180 degrees
Sideways, then rotated 90 degrees as it is advanced
Right side up, using a tongue depressor on the tongue
Through the nose until the flange meets the nostril

explanation: In children, the OPA is inserted right side up following the curve of the tongue while a tongue depressor presses the tongue down and forward. This avoids damaging the soft, easily injured palate that the adult rotation technique can tear.

distractorExplanations.a: Inserting upside down and rotating is the adult technique; in a child it can injure the soft palate and tear tissue.
distractorExplanations.b: The sideways 90-degree rotation is an alternative adult technique; children receive a tongue depressor and direct insertion.
distractorExplanations.d: Nasal insertion describes a nasopharyngeal airway, not an oropharyngeal airway.

prompt: An adult with increasing difficulty breathing is being reassessed. Which finding is a late sign of hypoxia?

options.text: Restlessness and anxiety
An increased heart rate
An increased respiratory rate and effort
Cyanosis of the lips and nail beds

explanation: Early hypoxia causes restlessness, anxiety, tachycardia, and tachypnea as the body compensates. Cyanosis is a late sign that appears only when oxygen saturation is already very low, so treatment should not wait for it.

distractorExplanations.a: Restlessness and anxiety are early signs of hypoxia, appearing as the brain first senses falling oxygen levels.
distractorExplanations.b: A rising heart rate is an early compensatory response to hypoxia, not a late finding.
distractorExplanations.c: A faster respiratory rate is an early attempt to compensate for low oxygen, before cyanosis develops.

prompt: A family found drowsy in a house with a generator running indoors all have SpO2 readings of 98-99%. How should you interpret these readings?

options.text: The readings may be falsely normal; give high-flow oxygen
Oxygenation is adequate, so oxygen can be withheld
The probes are faulty; change fingers and reassess later
Give oxygen only if a repeat reading falls below 94%

explanation: Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and standard pulse oximeters cannot tell it from oxygen, so SpO2 can look normal while tissues are hypoxic. Suspected CO exposure is treated with high-flow oxygen by nonrebreather, removal from the source, and transport.

distractorExplanations.b: Standard pulse oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxygenated hemoglobin, so a normal number does not rule out CO poisoning.
distractorExplanations.c: The device is working as designed; the problem is that it cannot distinguish carbon monoxide from oxygen on hemoglobin.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for a drop below 94% may never happen in CO poisoning even as tissue hypoxia worsens; give high-flow oxygen now.

prompt: Two EMRs are ventilating an apneic adult with a BVM. What is the most effective way to divide the tasks?

options.text: One squeezes the bag; the other applies continuous cricoid pressure
One seals and squeezes; the other counts breaths aloud
One seals the mask with both hands; the other squeezes the bag
Each rescuer takes over full BVM duties every 2 minutes

explanation: The two-rescuer BVM technique is preferred: one rescuer uses both hands to hold the mask seal and keep the airway open (jaw lift), while the other squeezes the bag over about 1 second per breath. A good seal is the main factor in adequate ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Routine cricoid pressure is no longer recommended; it can hinder ventilation and does not reliably prevent aspiration.
distractorExplanations.b: A single rescuer sealing and squeezing often leaks; the second rescuer is better used holding a two-handed seal.
distractorExplanations.d: Swapping every 2 minutes is the compression-rotation rule for CPR, not a technique for improving BVM ventilation.

prompt: During BVM ventilation of an apneic adult, the patient's upper abdomen becomes steadily more distended. What should you do?

options.text: Press on the upper abdomen to release the trapped air
Squeeze the bag harder to overcome the distension
Stop ventilating until the abdomen softens again
Reposition the airway and give slower, smaller breaths

explanation: Gastric distension comes from excessive volume, rate, or pressure, or a poorly opened airway. Reposition the head and jaw, give each breath over about 1 second with only enough volume for chest rise, have suction ready, and continue ventilating.

distractorExplanations.a: Pressing on a distended stomach can cause vomiting and aspiration in a patient who cannot protect the airway.
distractorExplanations.b: Harder squeezes force more air into the esophagus and worsen gastric distension and the risk of vomiting.
distractorExplanations.c: An apneic patient becomes hypoxic within minutes if ventilation stops; the technique is corrected, not abandoned.

prompt: An unresponsive adult has no pulse and takes an occasional gasping breath about every 10 seconds. How should you treat the breathing?

options.text: As absent breathing; begin CPR without delay
As adequate breathing; place in the recovery position
As slow breathing; give rescue breaths without compressions
As adequate breathing; apply a nonrebreather mask

explanation: Occasional gasps (agonal breathing) are a reflex of a dying brainstem, not effective ventilation. An unresponsive patient with no pulse and only gasping is in cardiac arrest, so begin high-quality CPR and apply the AED immediately.

distractorExplanations.b: Gasping is not effective breathing, and a pulseless patient in the recovery position receives no circulation at all.
distractorExplanations.c: Rescue breaths alone are for a patient who has a pulse; a pulseless patient needs chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: A nonrebreather supplies oxygen only to a patient who breathes effectively and has circulation; this patient has neither.

prompt: You are opening the airway of an unresponsive 4-month-old. Which head position is best?

options.text: Neck hyperextended, as for an adult
Chin flexed down toward the chest
Neutral position with a towel under the shoulders
A folded pillow under the back of the head to lift it

explanation: An infant's large occiput flexes the neck when lying flat. A thin towel under the shoulders brings the head to a neutral (sniffing) position, which aligns the airway without kinking the soft trachea through over-extension.

distractorExplanations.a: Hyperextending an infant's neck kinks the soft, flexible trachea and can obstruct the airway.
distractorExplanations.b: Flexing the chin toward the chest closes the infant airway, the same problem the large occiput already causes.
distractorExplanations.d: A pillow under the head flexes the neck further because infants already have a large occiput.

prompt: Firm direct pressure has not controlled severe bleeding from a lower-leg wound. What is your next step?

options.text: Add more gauze and press harder for 10 more minutes
Elevate the leg and compress the femoral pressure point
Apply a tourniquet directly over the wound site
Apply a tourniquet proximal to the wound

explanation: Life-threatening extremity bleeding that direct pressure cannot control calls for a tourniquet placed 2-3 inches above the wound (not over a joint) and tightened until bleeding stops. Note and report the time it was applied.

distractorExplanations.a: Once direct pressure has failed on severe extremity bleeding, more pressure time delays definitive control by tourniquet.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevation and pressure points are no longer recommended for severe bleeding; they delay tourniquet application.
distractorExplanations.c: A tourniquet goes 2–3 inches proximal to the wound, not on it, so it compresses the artery above the bleed.

prompt: A helmeted motorcycle rider is awake with stable vital signs after a crash. In which situation should the helmet be removed in the field?

options.text: The airway or breathing cannot be managed with it on
A cervical collar needs to be applied to the rider
The rider reports neck pain or tingling in the hands
The face shield must be lifted to assess the patient

explanation: A well-fitting helmet that permits airway access is left on with manual stabilization. It is removed, by two rescuers with inline stabilization, when the airway or breathing cannot be managed, vomit cannot be cleared, or it prevents proper immobilization.

distractorExplanations.b: Routine removal is not required; a snug helmet that allows airway access stays on with manual stabilization.
distractorExplanations.c: Neck pain or tingling suggests spinal injury, a reason to minimize movement, not to remove a helmet that allows airway care.
distractorExplanations.d: The shield or face mask can be lifted or removed without taking off the helmet; removal is reserved for airway problems.

prompt: After a rollover crash, which occupant most clearly needs spinal motion restriction under typical protocols?

options.text: Alert driver with no neck pain and a normal neurologic exam
Passenger with midline neck tenderness and tingling hands
Passenger with sore side-of-neck muscles and a normal exam
Alert driver with a seatbelt abrasion and no spinal pain

explanation: Common criteria for spinal motion restriction include midline spinal tenderness, a neurologic deficit such as numbness or tingling, altered mental status, intoxication, or a distracting injury. Protocols vary, and long backboards are increasingly reserved for extrication and movement.

distractorExplanations.a: An alert, reliable patient with no pain, no tenderness, and normal motor and sensory function meets common criteria for no restriction.
distractorExplanations.c: Lateral muscle soreness without midline tenderness or deficits does not by itself meet common spinal motion restriction criteria.
distractorExplanations.d: A seatbelt abrasion warrants chest and abdominal assessment, but without spinal pain, tenderness, or deficits it does not mandate restriction.

prompt: A patient with a deep thigh laceration has lost a large amount of blood. Which findings best fit hemorrhagic shock?

options.text: Warm, flushed skin with a slow pulse and a low blood pressure
High blood pressure, a slow pulse, and irregular breathing
Pale cool clammy skin, tachycardia, delayed capillary refill
Hot, dry, flushed skin with a rapid pulse and confusion

explanation: Blood loss triggers compensation: the heart speeds up and blood is shunted away from the skin, producing pale, cool, clammy skin and delayed capillary refill. Anxiety or altered mental status and, later, falling blood pressure follow as shock progresses.

distractorExplanations.a: Warm skin with bradycardia and hypotension describes neurogenic shock, not hemorrhagic (hypovolemic) shock.
distractorExplanations.b: That is Cushing's triad of rising intracranial pressure, not the picture of shock from hemorrhage.
distractorExplanations.d: Hot, dry skin with confusion suggests heat stroke; hemorrhage causes pale, cool, clammy skin.

prompt: A forearm fracture has bone protruding through the skin and is bleeding steadily. How should you manage it?

options.text: Realigning the exposed bone end back into the wound, then splinting it
Applying a tourniquet first for any bleeding open fracture
Wrapping tightly with an elastic bandage before splinting the arm
Covering with sterile dressing, controlling bleeding, and splinting

explanation: Never push exposed bone back in. Cover the wound with a sterile dressing, control bleeding with pressure around the bone end, splint the limb in the position found, and check circulation, motor, and sensation before and after splinting.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling exposed bone back into the wound contaminates deep tissue; cover it and splint without reducing it.
distractorExplanations.b: Most open-fracture bleeding stops with direct pressure; a tourniquet is reserved for life-threatening bleeding pressure cannot control.
distractorExplanations.c: A tight elastic wrap over an open fracture can cut off distal circulation; use a sterile dressing and check CMS before and after.

prompt: A hiker has a painful, swollen, deformed ankle after a fall. How should the EMR splint it?

options.text: Check CMS, splint in the position found, recheck CMS
Straighten the foot to neutral first, then splint it
Wrap the ankle snugly with an elastic bandage only
Apply a heat pack to the joint, then splint it loosely

explanation: Joint injuries are splinted in the position found, immobilizing the bones above and below. Circulation, motor function, and sensation (CMS) are checked before and after splinting so any compromise caused by the injury or the splint is detected.

distractorExplanations.b: Forcing a deformed joint into alignment can damage nerves and vessels; joints are splinted in the position found.
distractorExplanations.c: An elastic wrap compresses but does not immobilize the bones above and below the injury, and tight wraps can impair circulation.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat increases swelling in an acute injury; cold packs, not heat, are used after splinting to limit swelling and pain.

prompt: A worker has a metal rod impaled in the abdomen. How should the object be managed?

options.text: Immediate removal of the object to bandage the hole
Stabilization of the object in place and rapid transport
Cutting the rod flush with the skin to ease transport
Removal of the rod if bleeding soaks through the dressing

explanation: An impaled object may be plugging injured vessels, so it is left in place and stabilized with bulky dressings to prevent movement, with bleeding controlled around it. Removal is considered only if it blocks the airway or prevents CPR, per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Pulling the object out can release tamponaded vessels and cause uncontrolled internal and external bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Cutting transmits motion into the wound; an object is shortened only if needed, by rescuers, while it is stabilized.
distractorExplanations.d: Increased bleeding is controlled with pressure around the object; removal can release a tamponaded vessel and worsen hemorrhage.

prompt: Several patients were burned in a house fire. Which burn should receive priority cooling and transport consideration?

options.text: Superficial sunburn covering most of the back and both shoulders
Small full-thickness burn on the forearm with charred, painless, leathery skin
Partial-thickness burn to circumferential chest with singed nasal hairs
Partial-thickness burn to the front of one thigh, about 4% BSA

explanation: A circumferential chest burn can restrict chest expansion, and singed nasal hairs signal possible inhalation injury with airway swelling. Airway and breathing threats outrank larger or deeper burns elsewhere, so this patient needs priority care and rapid transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Superficial burns are not counted in critical burn size; airway involvement and circumferential burns take priority.
distractorExplanations.b: A small full-thickness burn away from critical areas is serious but lacks the airway threat of an inhalation injury.
distractorExplanations.d: About 4% partial-thickness on one thigh is a minor-to-moderate burn without airway or circumferential involvement.

prompt: After a fall onto a fence rail, a patient has rapidly worsening shortness of breath. Which findings suggest tension pneumothorax?

options.text: Muffled heart tones, distended neck veins, and low BP
Bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular breathing
Paradoxical movement of a chest segment on breathing
Tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds, and shock

explanation: Tension pneumothorax causes unilateral absent sounds, JVD, hypotension, and possible tracheal shift. Tracheal deviation is away from the affected side and is a late sign.

distractorExplanations.a: Muffled heart tones with JVD and hypotension are Beck's triad of cardiac tamponade; breath sounds stay equal.
distractorExplanations.b: That is Cushing's triad of rising intracranial pressure, not a sign of tension pneumothorax.
distractorExplanations.c: Paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment is the sign of a flail chest, not tension pneumothorax.

prompt: You are holding manual inline stabilization on a patient with a suspected neck injury. Which action is correct?

options.text: Maintain alignment until immobilization is coordinated
Release once a properly sized cervical collar is in place
Return the head to neutral even if pain or resistance occurs
Apply gentle upward traction to stretch the cervical spine

explanation: Manual stabilization continues until the patient is fully secured with spinal motion restriction by a coordinated team. A collar alone is not enough, the head is held without traction, and movement to neutral stops if it causes pain or resistance.

distractorExplanations.b: A collar alone does not fully restrict motion; manual stabilization continues until the patient is secured to the device.
distractorExplanations.c: Movement to neutral stops if it causes pain, resistance, or new deficits; the head is then held in the position found.
distractorExplanations.d: Traction on the neck can pull apart an unstable injury; the head is held inline without pulling.

prompt: A patient's finger was completely amputated by a saw. How should the amputated part be cared for?

options.text: Placed directly on ice in a cooler to slow tissue death
Wrapped in dry sterile gauze, sealed in a bag, kept cool
Submerged in a sealed container of saline and kept cool
Wrapped in gauze and kept at room temperature in a bag

explanation: Wrap the part in a dry sterile dressing (some local protocols moisten it with sterile saline), seal it in a plastic bag, label it, and keep it cool on cold packs or ice without direct ice contact. Transport it with the patient.

distractorExplanations.a: Direct ice contact freezes and destroys tissue; the bagged part rests on cold packs or ice without touching the ice.
distractorExplanations.c: Immersion waterlogs the tissue and hampers reattachment; the part is wrapped and bagged, never soaked.
distractorExplanations.d: Warm tissue deteriorates faster; the bagged part must be kept cool to extend the window for reattachment.

prompt: What is the main purpose of the primary assessment in a trauma patient?

options.text: Gather a complete SAMPLE history before any treatment
Find and treat immediate life threats in priority order
Locate and splint every fracture before moving anyone
Record a full set of baseline vital signs to trend

explanation: The primary assessment finds and fixes life threats as they are found: severe bleeding, airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure. Many current curricula put massive external bleeding first (XABCDE) because it kills fastest.

distractorExplanations.a: The SAMPLE history belongs to the secondary assessment and is gathered after life threats have been found and treated.
distractorExplanations.c: Splinting is secondary care; fractures are addressed only after airway, breathing, circulation, and severe bleeding are managed.
distractorExplanations.d: Baseline vitals are taken after the primary assessment; delaying treatment of a life threat to measure vitals is an error.

prompt: A driver struck the steering wheel and has several adjacent ribs broken in two places. Which finding do you expect?

options.text: Tracheal deviation and absent breath sounds on one side
Muffled heart sounds with distended neck veins and low BP
Inspiratory stridor from swelling of the upper airway
Paradoxical chest wall movement and respiratory distress

explanation: When two or more adjacent ribs break in two or more places, the free segment moves inward on inhalation and outward on exhalation (paradoxical motion). Breathing becomes painful and ineffective, so watch for hypoventilation and assist ventilations if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Tracheal shift with absent breath sounds is tension pneumothorax; flail chest shows a segment moving opposite the chest wall.
distractorExplanations.b: Muffled heart sounds, JVD, and hypotension point to cardiac tamponade, not a flail chest segment.
distractorExplanations.c: Stridor is an upper airway sign; a flail chest impairs chest wall mechanics and causes hypoventilation.

prompt: After you splint a fractured forearm, the radial pulse that was present before splinting is now absent. What should you do?

options.text: Loosen and adjust the splint, reassess, and expedite transport
Tighten the splint to control swelling and recheck in 15 minutes
Document it as expected after splinting and continue transport
Elevate the limb above the heart to improve circulation

explanation: A pulse that disappears after splinting usually means the splint or padding is compressing vessels. Loosen and readjust it, recheck circulation, motor, and sensation, and if the pulse does not return, treat it as a limb-threatening emergency.

distractorExplanations.b: A tight splint can occlude circulation; loss of a distal pulse after splinting means loosening and adjusting it now.
distractorExplanations.c: A new pulse loss is not expected; it signals compromised circulation that needs adjustment and urgent reassessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Elevation does not restore arterial flow blocked by a tight splint; loosen and readjust, then recheck the pulse.

prompt: You are dispatched to a two-car collision. Which elements belong in your scene size-up?

options.text: Standard precautions, chief complaint, SAMPLE history, and vitals
Standard precautions, scene safety, mechanism, number of patients
Primary survey of airway, breathing, and circulation
Scene safety, then a rapid trauma exam of the worst patient

explanation: Scene size-up comes before patient contact: take standard precautions, confirm the scene is safe, identify the mechanism of injury, count the patients, and request additional resources early. Patient assessment begins only after this.

distractorExplanations.a: Chief complaint, SAMPLE history, and vitals belong to patient assessment, which begins after the scene size-up.
distractorExplanations.c: The primary survey follows scene size-up; it is not part of evaluating hazards, mechanism, and resource needs.
distractorExplanations.d: Size-up must also count patients and request resources before committing to one patient's exam.

prompt: A stab wound in the groin is bleeding heavily, and a tourniquet cannot be applied there. How should you control the bleeding?

options.text: Elevate the leg and place an ice pack over the wound
Squeeze a pressure point above the wound without packing
Cover loosely with a dressing to avoid causing pain
Pack the wound tightly with gauze and hold firm pressure

explanation: Junctional wounds (groin, armpit, neck) cannot take a tourniquet. Pack gauze (hemostatic if available) firmly into the wound cavity down to the bleeding source and hold direct pressure for several minutes, then apply a pressure bandage.

distractorExplanations.a: Elevation and cold do not control arterial bleeding from a junctional wound and delay effective pressure.
distractorExplanations.b: Pressure points are no longer recommended; they are unreliable and delay direct pressure inside the wound.
distractorExplanations.c: A loose dressing hides ongoing hemorrhage; severe bleeding needs packing and firm, sustained pressure.

prompt: A tourniquet tightened 2-3 inches above a thigh wound has not stopped the bright red bleeding. What should you do?

options.text: Apply a second tourniquet just above the first
Loosen it and switch back to direct pressure
Remove it and reapply it directly over the wound
Elevate the leg and wait several minutes for clotting

explanation: If a correctly placed tourniquet is tightened fully and bleeding continues, apply a second tourniquet just proximal to (above) the first. Thighs often need two because of their muscle mass. Record the application times.

distractorExplanations.b: Loosening a tourniquet on uncontrolled bleeding restores flow to the wound; tourniquets are tightened, not released, in the field.
distractorExplanations.c: A tourniquet over the wound may not compress the artery and can damage tissue; it belongs proximal to the wound.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting for clotting while bright red blood flows allows fatal blood loss; add tourniquet pressure now.

prompt: A patient has an open chest wound that bubbles and sucks air with each breath. Which dressing is preferred?

options.text: Bulky gauze packed deep into the wound
A moist sterile dressing taped on all sides loosely
A vented chest seal, monitoring for tension
A tight elastic wrap around the entire chest

explanation: An open pneumothorax is sealed with a vented chest seal or an occlusive dressing. Watch closely for tension pneumothorax (worsening distress, falling BP); if it develops, briefly lift (burp) the seal per protocol to release trapped air.

distractorExplanations.a: Packing is for extremity and junctional bleeding; packing a chest wound does not seal it and may enter the pleural space.
distractorExplanations.b: A loosely taped moist dressing lets air keep entering the chest; the seal must be occlusive.
distractorExplanations.d: A tight chest wrap restricts chest expansion and worsens ventilation without sealing the wound.

prompt: Loops of bowel are protruding from a laceration in a patient's abdomen. How should you manage them?

options.text: Gently push the organs back inside the abdomen
Cover with dry gauze and pack it down firmly
Leave them uncovered and apply cold packs around the wound edges
Cover with a moist sterile dressing and an occlusive layer

explanation: An abdominal evisceration is covered with a sterile dressing moistened with sterile saline, then an occlusive layer to keep the organs moist and warm. Position the patient with knees flexed if tolerated, treat for shock, and transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Replacing organs introduces contamination and can injure them further; eviscerated organs are never pushed back.
distractorExplanations.b: Dry gauze sticks to and dries out exposed bowel, and packing it down damages the organs.
distractorExplanations.c: Uncovered organs dry out, lose heat, and become contaminated; cold packs worsen heat loss.

prompt: An adult has partial-thickness burns over the entire front of the chest and abdomen and the entire right arm. Using the rule of nines, what is the estimated burned body surface area?
explanation: In the adult rule of nines, the entire anterior trunk is 18% and each entire arm is 9%. Anterior trunk 18% + right arm 9% = 27% BSA. Superficial burns are not counted in this estimate.

distractorExplanations.a: Eighteen percent counts only the anterior trunk and leaves out the 9% for the entire right arm.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty-six percent counts the whole trunk front and back (or two arms); only the front of the trunk and one arm are burned.
distractorExplanations.d: Forty-five percent adds regions that are not burned; the anterior trunk (18%) and one arm (9%) total 27%.

prompt: A cook spilled hot oil on his forearm 2 minutes ago. Which initial burn care is best?

options.text: Cool with clean running water, then apply a dry sterile dressing
Apply ice directly to the burn for 20 minutes, then cover it
Apply butter or ointment to seal the skin, then cover it loosely
Open any blisters to release the fluid, then cover with dry gauze

explanation: Stop the burning process and cool a small burn with clean, cool running water (first-aid guidance is about 20 minutes, avoiding hypothermia with large burns), remove jewelry, then cover with a dry sterile dressing. Never use ice, butter, or ointments.

distractorExplanations.b: Ice causes vasoconstriction and frostbite-like injury to already damaged skin, deepening the burn.
distractorExplanations.c: Butter and ointments trap heat, increase infection risk, and must be removed at the hospital.
distractorExplanations.d: Intact blisters protect against infection; breaking them opens the wound to contamination.

prompt: A worker's arms are covered in dry lime powder from a broken bag. How should you decontaminate the skin?

options.text: Flush immediately without brushing off the powder
Brush off the powder, then flush with large amounts of water
Neutralize the powder with vinegar before flushing
Wipe with a damp towel, then cover the arms with a dry dressing

explanation: Dry chemicals such as lime are brushed off first (with PPE), then the skin is flushed with large volumes of water for an extended period. Remove contaminated clothing and jewelry, and continue flushing en route if needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Wetting a large amount of dry lime first creates a caustic solution on the skin before most of the powder is removed.
distractorExplanations.c: Neutralizing agents produce heat and worsen the burn; plain water is the decontaminating agent.
distractorExplanations.d: A damp towel activates the lime without removing it, and covering the skin traps the chemical against it.

prompt: A lineman lies unresponsive next to a downed power line. What is your first action?

options.text: Move the wire away using a dry wooden branch or broom handle
Drag the patient away by his clothing
Keep away until the utility shuts off the power
Begin CPR, then call the power company

explanation: Downed lines and anything touching them may be energized, and the ground around them can carry current. Stay well back, keep others away, and do not approach until the utility confirms the power is off; then assess for cardiac arrest and burns.

distractorExplanations.a: Wood and other improvised tools can conduct high voltage; rescuers do not handle wires themselves.
distractorExplanations.b: Touching the patient while he may still be energized, or crossing energized ground, can electrocute the rescuer.
distractorExplanations.d: Approaching to start CPR before the power is confirmed off puts the rescuer at risk of electrocution.

prompt: After a fall, a patient has bruising behind both ears and clear fluid draining from the nose. Which injury do these findings suggest?

options.text: A concussion without any fracture
A broken nose (nasal fracture)
A fracture of the cervical spine
A basilar skull fracture

explanation: Bruising behind the ears (Battle's sign), bruising around the eyes (raccoon eyes), and clear fluid (cerebrospinal fluid) from the nose or ears indicate a basilar skull fracture. Do not pack the nose or insert a nasal airway.

distractorExplanations.a: A concussion causes confusion or memory loss but does not produce bruising behind the ears or cerebrospinal fluid leakage.
distractorExplanations.b: A nasal fracture causes bleeding and deformity of the nose, not clear fluid with bruising behind the ears.
distractorExplanations.c: A cervical spine fracture causes neck pain or neurologic deficits, not mastoid bruising or fluid from the nose.

prompt: A head-injured patient does not respond to your voice but moans and pulls away when you pinch the trapezius. Which AVPU level is this?

options.text: A - alert
V - responds when spoken to aloud
P - responds to painful stimuli
U - unresponsive

explanation: AVPU grades responsiveness: Alert, responds to Verbal stimuli, responds to Painful stimuli, or Unresponsive. A patient who ignores voice but moans and withdraws from a trapezius pinch is at the P level, which is a significant decrease.

distractorExplanations.a: An alert patient has open eyes and interacts spontaneously without being prompted.
distractorExplanations.b: A verbal-level patient responds when spoken to; this patient responds only to the painful stimulus.
distractorExplanations.d: An unresponsive patient makes no response even to pain; this patient moans and withdraws.

prompt: A pedestrian struck by a car has pelvic pain and signs of shock. How should you handle the suspected pelvic fracture?

options.text: Avoid rocking it; apply a binder at the greater trochanters
Compress and rock the pelvis firmly to confirm it is unstable
Apply a pelvic binder around the waist at the iliac crests
Raise the legs 12 inches to treat the shock first

explanation: An unstable pelvic fracture can bleed massively into the pelvis. Avoid repeated movement or rocking, stabilize with a pelvic binder or sheet centered over the greater trochanters (per protocol), treat for shock, and transport rapidly.

distractorExplanations.b: Rocking an unstable pelvis can dislodge clots and worsen life-threatening internal bleeding; it is never repeated.
distractorExplanations.c: A binder placed at the waist does not close the pelvic ring; it must be centered over the greater trochanters.
distractorExplanations.d: Leg elevation moves the fractured pelvis and is no longer routine shock care for suspected pelvic injury.

prompt: A cyclist fell on an outstretched arm and has a deformed, painful collarbone. Which immobilization is most appropriate?

options.text: A rigid board splint along the forearm only
A sling and swathe holding the arm against the chest
Traction on the arm to realign the collarbone
An elastic wrap around the shoulder, leaving the arm free to move

explanation: Clavicle and shoulder injuries are immobilized with a sling to support the arm's weight and a swathe to hold the arm against the chest. Check circulation, motor function, and sensation in the hand before and after.

distractorExplanations.a: A forearm board splint immobilizes the wrist and forearm but leaves the clavicle and shoulder free to move.
distractorExplanations.c: EMRs do not apply traction to realign a clavicle; manipulation can injure the vessels and nerves beneath it.
distractorExplanations.d: An elastic wrap without arm support lets the arm's weight pull on the fracture with every movement.

prompt: A metal shard is impaled in a worker's right eye. How should you manage it?

options.text: Remove it gently and patch the injured eye
Cover only the injured eye with firm pressure
Stabilize it with a cup and cover both eyes
Flush the eye with water to wash it free

explanation: Stabilize an impaled eye object with bulky dressing and a protective cup without pressing on the globe, and cover the uninjured eye as well. The eyes move together, so covering both reduces movement of the injured eye.

distractorExplanations.a: Removing an impaled object can cause loss of eye contents and permanent blindness; it is stabilized in place.
distractorExplanations.b: Firm pressure on an injured globe can force out its contents, and the uninjured eye must also be covered.
distractorExplanations.d: Irrigation is for chemical exposures; flushing an impaled object can move it and worsen the injury.

prompt: A worker splashed a cleaning chemical into his left eye. How should you irrigate it?

options.text: Outward from the inner corner for about 2 minutes
From the outer corner toward the nose for at least 20 minutes
With a neutralizing solution, then patch the eye
Outward from the inner corner for at least 15-20 minutes

explanation: Hold the eyelids open and flush with clean water or saline from the inner corner (near the nose) outward, so runoff does not reach the other eye. Continue for at least 15-20 minutes, longer for alkalis or per protocol, and remove contact lenses if possible.

distractorExplanations.a: Two minutes is far too short; chemicals keep injuring the eye unless flushing continues for an extended period.
distractorExplanations.b: Flushing toward the nose can carry the chemical into the uninjured eye; flow goes from the inner corner outward.
distractorExplanations.c: Neutralizing agents can cause heat and further injury; plain water or saline is used, and patching comes later.

prompt: A patient has a spontaneous nosebleed with no trauma. Which positioning and care do you provide?

options.text: Sit leaning forward and pinch the soft part of the nose
Tilt the head back and pinch the bony bridge of the nose
Lie flat and pack the nostril tightly with gauze
Lean back and apply ice to the back of the neck

explanation: Have the patient sit up and lean forward so blood drains out rather than into the throat, and pinch the soft, fleshy part of the nose firmly for about 10-15 minutes. Most anterior nosebleeds stop with sustained pressure.

distractorExplanations.b: Tilting the head back sends blood down the throat, causing nausea, vomiting, and aspiration risk, and the bridge is not where bleeding occurs.
distractorExplanations.c: Lying flat lets blood run into the airway, and packing the nose is not an EMR intervention.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaning back lets blood drain into the throat, and ice on the neck does not compress the bleeding vessels.

prompt: You find an unresponsive adult without pulse. After activating EMS and getting an AED, you should

options.text: Give 2 rescue breaths, then check the pulse again
Give rescue breaths at 1 every 6 seconds
Start chest compressions at 100–120/min
Start compressions at 60–80/min to limit rib injury

explanation: BLS for adult cardiac arrest emphasizes immediate high-quality compressions and early AED. Allow full chest recoil between compressions.

distractorExplanations.a: Adult CPR starts with compressions (C-A-B); repeating pulse checks delays compressions in a confirmed arrest.
distractorExplanations.b: Rescue breathing alone is for a patient who has a pulse; a pulseless patient needs chest compressions.
distractorExplanations.d: The guideline rate is 100–120 per minute; slower compressions reduce blood flow generated during CPR.

prompt: A bystander asks what the FAST stroke screen checks. Which list is correct?

options.text: Facial droop, arm drift, speech, and current blood glucose level
Facial droop, abdominal pain, slurred speech, and temperature
Fixed pupils, abnormal posturing, seizures, and trauma
Facial droop, arm drift, speech difficulty, and time of onset

explanation: FAST stands for Face (droop), Arms (drift), Speech (slurred or absent), and Time: the time of onset or last known well. That time decides eligibility for clot-dissolving treatment, so it must be documented and passed to the receiving facility.

distractorExplanations.a: Glucose is checked to rule out hypoglycemia mimics, but the T in FAST is time of onset (last known well).
distractorExplanations.b: The A in FAST is arm drift, not abdominal pain, and temperature is not a FAST element.
distractorExplanations.c: Pupils and posturing are head-injury and GCS findings, not the elements of FAST stroke screening.

prompt: A diabetic patient is confused, sweaty, and shaky, with a glucose reading of 52 mg/dL. What should you do?

options.text: Administer oral glucose if awake and able to swallow safely
Assist with the patient's own insulin pen to correct the sugar
Wait to recheck glucose in 15 minutes before treating
Withhold oral glucose because the patient is confused

explanation: A symptomatic low glucose is treated promptly. If the patient is awake enough to follow commands, can protect the airway, and swallows safely, give oral glucose per local protocol, then reassess mental status and recheck glucose about 15 minutes later.

distractorExplanations.b: Insulin lowers glucose further; it treats hyperglycemia and would worsen this patient's hypoglycemia.
distractorExplanations.c: A symptomatic glucose of 52 mg/dL is treated now; the 15-minute recheck comes after giving oral glucose.
distractorExplanations.d: Confusion alone does not bar oral glucose if the patient is awake, follows commands, and swallows safely.

prompt: A patient stung by a bee develops wheezing, hives, and a blood pressure of 78/50. What treatment is required?

options.text: Oral diphenhydramine and transport if the hives spread
Epinephrine auto-injector per protocol and rapid transport
High-flow oxygen and observation for 30 minutes on scene
Scraping the stinger, then rapid transport without medication

explanation: Wheezing plus hypotension means systemic anaphylaxis. Intramuscular epinephrine, by the patient's prescribed auto-injector or per protocol, reverses bronchospasm and vasodilation; give it without delay, transport rapidly, and be ready to repeat per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Antihistamines do not reverse hypotension or bronchospasm; anaphylaxis needs epinephrine first.
distractorExplanations.c: Oxygen supports but does not reverse anaphylaxis; delaying epinephrine and transport worsens outcomes.
distractorExplanations.d: Removing the stinger is fine but secondary; wheeze and hypotension mean systemic anaphylaxis needing epinephrine.

prompt: Your local protocol lets EMRs help patients take their own prescribed nitroglycerin for chest pain. Which patient may you assist?

options.text: BP 138/84, no erectile-dysfunction drugs, own nitroglycerin
BP 142/90, took sildenafil 12 hours ago, own nitroglycerin
BP 84/50, no erectile-dysfunction drugs, own nitroglycerin
BP 136/80, no erectile-dysfunction drugs, wife's nitroglycerin

explanation: Nitroglycerin dilates vessels and lowers blood pressure. Before assisting, confirm it is the patient's own prescription, that systolic BP meets the protocol minimum, and that no PDE-5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil) has been taken recently. National EMR scope may not include this, so follow local protocol.

distractorExplanations.b: Sildenafil taken within about 24 hours (48 for tadalafil) combines with nitroglycerin to cause severe hypotension, so it is withheld.
distractorExplanations.c: A systolic pressure below the protocol minimum (commonly 90-100 mmHg) is a contraindication, because nitroglycerin lowers BP further.
distractorExplanations.d: Only the patient's own prescribed nitroglycerin may be assisted; another person's medication is never given.

prompt: A roofer faints on a hot afternoon but is alert within a minute, with cool, moist skin. What is the most likely problem and first step?

options.text: Heat stroke needing ice-water immersion
A seizure disorder; protect from injury
Simple fainting; no assessment is needed
Heat-related illness; move to cool area

explanation: Brief fainting with quick recovery and cool, moist skin fits heat syncope or heat exhaustion. Move the patient to a cool place, loosen clothing, and assess hydration, perfusion, and mental status while watching for progression to heat stroke.

distractorExplanations.a: Heat stroke presents with persistent altered mental status and hot skin; rapid recovery points to heat syncope or exhaustion.
distractorExplanations.b: A brief faint with quick recovery in the heat fits heat syncope; a seizure is typically followed by a postictal period.
distractorExplanations.c: Even with rapid recovery, syncope needs assessment for heat illness, dehydration, and cardiac causes.
