prompt: Seizure activity has stopped, and the patient is postictal but breathing adequately. What should you do now?

options.text: Place in recovery position, protect from injury, monitor airway
Restrain the limbs loosely to prevent a second seizure
Insert an oral airway to hold the airway open while drowsy
Keep the patient supine and recheck the vital signs in 15 minutes

explanation: Post-seizure care focuses on airway, protection, oxygen if needed, and evaluation. Time the event and arrange transport for evaluation.

distractorExplanations.b: Restraint does not prevent recurrent seizures and can cause injury; protect the patient from surrounding objects instead.
distractorExplanations.c: An OPA triggers gagging and vomiting in a postictal patient with a gag reflex; positioning and suction manage the airway.
distractorExplanations.d: Supine positioning lets secretions pool in the airway; the recovery position with continuous airway monitoring is needed.

prompt: Which set of vital signs suggests decompensated shock in a patient with severe vomiting and diarrhea?

options.text: Heart rate 118, BP 124/82, cool pale skin, anxious but alert
Heart rate 130, BP 86/60, cool skin, altered mental status
Heart rate 60, BP 168/98, slow irregular breathing, drowsy
Heart rate 104, BP 132/88, flushed warm skin, alert

explanation: Decompensated shock begins when compensation fails: blood pressure falls despite a fast heart rate, perfusion worsens, and the underperfused brain produces altered mental status. Hypotension is the dividing line from compensated shock.

distractorExplanations.a: Tachycardia and cool skin with a normal BP is compensated shock; decompensation adds falling BP and altered mentation.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypertension with a slow pulse and irregular breathing is Cushing's triad of rising ICP, not shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Mild tachycardia with a normal BP and warm skin lacks the hypotension and poor perfusion of decompensated shock.

prompt: An adult asthma patient who was wheezing loudly now has a silent chest and looks exhausted. What does this indicate?

options.text: Improving airflow after the inhaler has taken effect
An anxiety reaction causing shallow breathing
Impending respiratory failure requiring urgent transport
A mild attack that can be managed on scene with rest and oxygen

explanation: A silent chest means so little air is moving that wheezes can no longer be heard, and exhaustion means the breathing muscles are failing. This is impending respiratory arrest: assist ventilations as needed, request ALS early, and transport rapidly.

distractorExplanations.a: Less wheezing with exhaustion means too little air is moving to wheeze; a silent chest is ominous, not improvement.
distractorExplanations.b: Exhaustion with a silent chest is respiratory failure; attributing it to anxiety delays ventilation and transport.
distractorExplanations.d: A silent chest is a late, life-threatening sign; it calls for ventilatory support and rapid transport, not on-scene care.

prompt: A patient with pinpoint pupils is breathing 4 times per minute after a suspected opioid overdose. What does EMR care include?

options.text: Sternal rubs and loud verbal stimulation to rouse the patient, then transport
Naloxone first, holding ventilations until it takes effect
High-flow oxygen by nonrebreather mask, then transport
Airway/ventilation support, naloxone per protocol, and transport

explanation: Respiratory depression is what kills in opioid overdose. Open the airway and ventilate with a BVM and oxygen, give naloxone (intranasal or auto-injector) per protocol, and keep ventilating until breathing is adequate; naloxone can wear off before the opioid does.

distractorExplanations.a: Stimulation does not correct respiratory depression; inadequate breathing needs BVM ventilation and naloxone per protocol.
distractorExplanations.b: Naloxone takes minutes and may be insufficient; ventilate with a BVM while naloxone is given.
distractorExplanations.c: A nonrebreather cannot help slow, shallow breathing; respiratory depression requires assisted BVM ventilation.

prompt: A patient with chest pain reports a true aspirin allergy (hives and wheezing the last time). What should the EMR do about aspirin?

options.text: Give it if protocol allows after an allergy assessment
Give a reduced 81 mg dose to lower the reaction risk
Give oral diphenhydramine first, then give the aspirin
Withhold it, monitor closely and arrange rapid transport

explanation: A true aspirin allergy is a contraindication, so the EMR withholds aspirin, keeps the patient at rest, monitors breathing and vital signs, and arranges rapid transport with ALS notified. Chest pain still needs definitive care even when aspirin cannot be given.

distractorExplanations.a: A documented aspirin allergy is itself a contraindication; no protocol step or allergy assessment makes aspirin appropriate for this patient.
distractorExplanations.b: A lower dose does not prevent an allergic reaction; a true aspirin allergy rules out aspirin at any dose.
distractorExplanations.c: Premedicating with an antihistamine does not make aspirin safe in a true allergy and is outside EMR scope of practice.

prompt: A runner who collapsed in a summer race is confused, with hot skin and a very high body temperature. What is the likely condition?

options.text: Heat exhaustion needing rest and oral fluids
Heat stroke requiring rapid cooling and transport
Hypoglycemia needing oral glucose and observation
Heat cramps relieved by stretching and electrolytes

explanation: Heat stroke is defined by central nervous system dysfunction with a dangerously high core temperature; the skin may be hot and dry or still sweaty. It is life-threatening, so start rapid cooling (cold-water immersion where available) and transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Heat exhaustion keeps mental status near normal with moist skin; altered mentation with hot, dry skin is heat stroke.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypoglycemia causes cool, clammy skin; fever with hot, dry skin and altered mentation points to heat stroke.
distractorExplanations.d: Heat cramps cause painful muscle spasms with normal mentation, not altered mental status and hot, dry skin.

prompt: You are helping a patient use her prescribed epinephrine auto-injector. Where should it be injected?

options.text: Upper outer buttock (gluteal muscle)
Back of the upper arm (subcutaneous)
Outer mid-thigh (vastus lateralis)
Inner thigh near the femoral artery

explanation: Epinephrine auto-injectors are designed for intramuscular injection into the outer (anterolateral) thigh, the vastus lateralis, which absorbs quickly; they can be given through clothing and are held in place for the time in the device instructions.

distractorExplanations.a: Auto-injectors are designed for the anterolateral thigh; gluteal injection risks fat deposition or sciatic nerve injury.
distractorExplanations.b: Subcutaneous absorption is slower; epinephrine auto-injectors deliver an IM dose into the lateral thigh.
distractorExplanations.d: The inner thigh lies over major vessels and nerves; the auto-injector goes into the outer (lateral) thigh.

prompt: A patient has severe abdominal pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen. Which care is the priority?

options.text: Small sips of water and an antacid, then monitor vitals
Lay supine with legs straight and palpate the painful area first
Apply a heat pack to the abdomen and observe on scene
Keep NPO, monitor vitals, position of comfort, rapid transport

explanation: A rigid abdomen suggests peritonitis or internal bleeding that may need surgery. Give nothing by mouth, let the patient stay in a position of comfort (often knees drawn up), monitor for shock, and arrange rapid transport.

distractorExplanations.a: A rigid abdomen may need surgery; anything by mouth risks vomiting and aspiration, so the patient stays NPO.
distractorExplanations.b: Abdominal pain patients usually prefer knees flexed, and the painful quadrant is palpated last to avoid guarding.
distractorExplanations.c: Heat can mask worsening signs, and a rigid abdomen suggests a surgical emergency that needs rapid transport.

prompt: A short-of-breath patient has an SpO2 of 88% on room air. What should this reading prompt?

options.text: Oxygen per protocol and reassessment of work of breathing
Recheck the probe placement and wait for symptoms to worsen
Oxygen only if the reading falls below 85% on recheck
BVM ventilation even though breathing is adequate

explanation: An SpO2 below about 94% with symptoms means hypoxemia. Give supplemental oxygen per protocol, titrated to the target range, and reassess work of breathing, mental status, and readings; switch to BVM ventilation only if breathing becomes inadequate.

distractorExplanations.b: Checking probe placement is reasonable, but a symptomatic patient at 88% needs oxygen now, not delayed treatment.
distractorExplanations.c: Below about 94% in a symptomatic patient, oxygen is indicated; waiting for 85% delays needed treatment.
distractorExplanations.d: BVM ventilation is for inadequate breathing; adequate breathing with hypoxemia needs supplemental oxygen.

prompt: During adult CPR, how deep should chest compressions be?

options.text: 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5-4 cm)
1.5 to 2 inches (4-5 cm)
2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm)
2.5 to 3 inches (6-7.5 cm)

explanation: AHA guidance for adults is a compression depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not more than about 2.4 inches (6 cm), at 100-120 per minute, allowing full chest recoil and minimizing interruptions.

distractorExplanations.a: One to 1.5 inches is too shallow to generate adequate blood flow in an adult; it is closer to infant depth.
distractorExplanations.b: One and a half to 2 inches approximates infant and child depth, short of the adult minimum of 2 inches.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressing more than about 2.4 inches increases injury risk without improving blood flow in an adult.

prompt: Two rescuers are performing CPR on an unresponsive 6-year-old with no pulse. Which compression-to-ventilation ratio do they use?
explanation: AHA guidance: single rescuers use 30:2 for all ages, but two rescuers caring for an infant or child use 15:2 to provide more ventilation, since pediatric arrests are usually caused by respiratory failure.

distractorExplanations.a: Fifteen compressions to one breath is not an AHA ratio; two breaths follow each cycle of 15 compressions.
distractorExplanations.c: Thirty to one is not an AHA ratio; each cycle ends with two breaths.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty to two is the single-rescuer ratio for children and the ratio for adults, not two-rescuer child CPR.

prompt: Two trained rescuers are giving CPR to an infant. Which compression technique is recommended?

options.text: Two fingers placed on the breastbone just below the nipples
Two-thumb encircling hands on the lower half of the sternum
The heel of both hands on the center of the chest
One hand on the upper sternum near the sternal notch

explanation: For infants, two rescuers use the two-thumb encircling-hands technique on the lower half of the sternum, compressing about 1.5 inches (4 cm), one-third of chest depth. It produces better depth and blood flow than two fingers.

distractorExplanations.a: Two-finger compressions are often too shallow; 2025 AHA guidance dropped them in favor of two-thumb or one-hand technique.
distractorExplanations.c: Two hands are the adult technique and are too forceful and too large for an infant's chest.
distractorExplanations.d: Compressions on the upper sternum near the notch miss the heart and risk injury; the lower half of the sternum is used.

prompt: You need an AED for a pulseless 4-year-old but have only adult pads. What should you do?

options.text: Withhold the AED and continue CPR alone
Cut the adult pads in half to fit the chest
Use the adult pads, front and back if they would touch
Use a single adult pad placed on the center of the chest

explanation: Use pediatric pads or attenuator for children under 8 if available; if not, use adult pads. If adult pads would touch on a small chest, place one in front (center chest) and one on the back between the shoulder blades.

distractorExplanations.a: Defibrillation saves lives in shockable pediatric arrests; adult pads are used when pediatric pads are unavailable.
distractorExplanations.b: Cutting pads destroys the electrode and its wiring, so no shock can be delivered.
distractorExplanations.d: A shock needs two pads to complete the circuit through the heart; one pad cannot defibrillate.

prompt: A pulseless swimmer has just been pulled from a pool. What should you do before applying AED pads?

options.text: Wait until the chest has air-dried completely
Place the pads on the back to avoid the wet chest
Skip the AED because water conducts the current
Move him out of standing water and dry the chest

explanation: Water can divert current across the skin and reduce the shock reaching the heart. Move the patient out of standing water, quickly dry the chest, apply the pads, and ensure no one is touching the patient during analysis and shock.

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting for the chest to air-dry delays defibrillation; wipe it dry quickly with a towel instead.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving pads to the back does not solve a wet chest and places them incorrectly for most patients.
distractorExplanations.c: Water is not a reason to withhold the AED; moving the patient out of water and drying the chest makes it safe.

prompt: An unresponsive adult is not breathing normally. How long should you spend checking for a pulse before starting CPR?

options.text: No more than 5 seconds
No more than 10 seconds
Between 15 and 20 seconds
About 30 seconds

explanation: AHA guidance limits the pulse check to no more than 10 seconds, done while checking breathing. If a definite pulse is not felt in that time in an unresponsive patient who is not breathing normally, start compressions.

distractorExplanations.a: Five seconds is shorter than the AHA guideline and may miss a slow pulse, but the limit is 10 seconds.
distractorExplanations.c: Spending 15-20 seconds on a pulse check delays compressions; begin CPR if no definite pulse is felt in 10 seconds.
distractorExplanations.d: Thirty seconds without compressions sharply lowers survival; pulse checks are limited to 10 seconds.

prompt: A hiker found outdoors is shivering, confused, and has cold skin. How should you handle and warm him?

options.text: Handle gently, remove wet clothing, and warm passively
Rub the arms and legs vigorously to restore circulation
Give him coffee to warm him from the inside
Walk him around briskly to generate body heat

explanation: Hypothermia care: move the patient to a warm environment, handle gently (rough movement can trigger ventricular fibrillation), remove wet clothing, insulate with dry blankets, and warm passively. Give nothing by mouth to a confused patient.

distractorExplanations.b: Rubbing the extremities can injure cold tissue and push cold blood to the core; handle the patient gently.
distractorExplanations.c: Caffeine and hot drinks are not given to a confused patient who may aspirate; warming is external and passive.
distractorExplanations.d: Exertion in a hypothermic patient can trigger dysrhythmias as cold blood returns to the heart.

prompt: A 72-year-old diabetic woman reports sudden weakness, nausea, and shortness of breath but no chest pain. What should the EMR suspect?

options.text: Simple food poisoning that needs fluids
A possible heart attack with atypical signs
Anxiety, because there is no chest pain
Seasonal flu that can be managed with rest at home

explanation: Women, older adults, and diabetics often have atypical heart attack symptoms such as weakness, nausea, shortness of breath, or fatigue without classic chest pain. Treat as possible acute coronary syndrome: rest, oxygen if hypoxic, and rapid transport.

distractorExplanations.a: Assuming food poisoning in an older diabetic with dyspnea and weakness can miss a heart attack.
distractorExplanations.c: Absence of chest pain does not rule out a heart attack; attributing these symptoms to anxiety delays care.
distractorExplanations.d: Sudden weakness with shortness of breath needs evaluation for a cardiac cause, not home care.

prompt: A toddler swallowed drain cleaner about 10 minutes ago and is alert, drooling, and crying. What should you do?

options.text: Induce vomiting to get the chemical out
Give vinegar or juice to neutralize it
Contact poison control or medical direction
Give activated charcoal by mouth right away

explanation: For an ingested caustic, do not induce vomiting or give neutralizers. Assess the airway (drooling suggests oral burns), bring the container, contact poison control or medical direction per protocol, and transport while watching for airway swelling.

distractorExplanations.a: Vomiting a caustic burns the esophagus a second time and risks aspiration; vomiting is never induced.
distractorExplanations.b: Neutralizing agents create heat and further tissue injury; nothing is given by mouth without direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Activated charcoal does not bind caustics, obscures endoscopy, and is not an EMR treatment.

prompt: A woman in labor with her third child says she must push, and the baby's head is visible at the vaginal opening during contractions. What should you do?

options.text: Have her cross her legs and transport at once
Ask her to use the bathroom first
Drive with lights and siren to beat the birth
Prepare to deliver the baby at the scene

explanation: Crowning plus the urge to push, especially in a woman who has given birth before, means delivery is imminent. Request additional help, put on PPE, position the mother, and prepare the OB kit to deliver on scene rather than transporting.

distractorExplanations.a: Crossing the legs or holding the baby back can injure mother and baby; crowning means birth is imminent.
distractorExplanations.b: The urge to push feels like needing a bowel movement; going to the toilet can lead to an unattended birth.
distractorExplanations.c: Crowning in a multiparous mother means birth within minutes; delivering in a moving vehicle is riskier.

prompt: A baby has just been delivered and is limp and not crying. What is your first action?

options.text: Dry, warm, and stimulate while positioning the airway
Begin chest compressions at about 120 per minute
Clamp and cut the cord before any other care
Suction deeply for 30 seconds to clear the mouth and throat

explanation: Initial newborn care: dry the baby thoroughly, keep warm, position the airway (neutral), clear secretions only if needed, and stimulate by rubbing the back or flicking the soles. Most newborns respond; reassess breathing and heart rate next.

distractorExplanations.b: Compressions start only if the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation; drying and stimulation come first.
distractorExplanations.c: The cord can wait; warming, drying, and opening the airway are the immediate priorities for a limp newborn.
distractorExplanations.d: Routine deep suctioning can cause bradycardia; suction briefly only if secretions obstruct breathing.

prompt: After drying and stimulating, a newborn has a heart rate of 80 per minute and only weak, gasping breaths. What is the next step?

options.text: Start chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Begin positive-pressure ventilation with a BVM
Give blow-by oxygen near the face and observe the baby
Continue drying and recheck in 5 minutes

explanation: In newborn resuscitation, apnea, gasping, or a heart rate below 100 per minute after initial steps calls for positive-pressure ventilation at about 40-60 breaths per minute. Compressions (3:1) begin only if the heart rate stays below 60 despite effective ventilation.

distractorExplanations.a: Compressions are started only if the heart rate remains below 60 per minute despite 30 seconds of effective ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Blow-by oxygen helps a baby who is breathing adequately; gasping with a heart rate under 100 needs ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting 5 minutes while a newborn gasps with a heart rate under 100 allows hypoxia to worsen.

prompt: During labor, a loop of umbilical cord is protruding from the vagina before the baby. What should you do?

options.text: Push the cord back into the vagina gently
Pull gently on the cord to speed delivery
Elevate her hips and lift the baby off the cord
Have the mother push hard with each contraction to deliver quickly

explanation: A prolapsed cord is compressed between the baby and the birth canal, cutting off oxygen. Position the mother with hips elevated (knee-chest or Trendelenburg), insert a gloved hand to lift the presenting part off the cord, keep the cord moist, and transport rapidly.

distractorExplanations.a: Pushing the cord back can damage it and does not relieve pressure from the presenting part.
distractorExplanations.b: Pulling on the cord can tear it or worsen compression, cutting off the baby's blood supply.
distractorExplanations.d: Pushing drives the baby's head harder against the cord, compressing it further.

prompt: A woman who is 34 weeks pregnant becomes dizzy and pale while lying flat on her back. How should you position her?

options.text: Supine with her legs raised 12 inches
Flat on her back with the head lowered
Sitting upright and leaning forward
Tilted or lying on her left side

explanation: In late pregnancy, lying supine lets the uterus compress the inferior vena cava, reducing return of blood to the heart (supine hypotensive syndrome). Positioning her on her left side, or tilting her left, relieves the pressure.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising the legs while supine leaves the uterus compressing the vena cava, which is causing the problem.
distractorExplanations.b: Head-down supine positioning keeps the uterus on the vena cava and may worsen breathing.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaning forward does not relieve caval compression and can be unstable for a dizzy patient.

prompt: From the doorway, you use the Pediatric Assessment Triangle on a sick toddler. Which three components do you observe?

options.text: Appearance, work of breathing, and skin circulation
Airway, breathing, and circulation checked by touch
Pulse rate, blood pressure, and capillary refill
Responsiveness, pupil size, and body temperature

explanation: The Pediatric Assessment Triangle is a hands-off first impression: Appearance (tone, interactiveness, look, speech/cry), Work of breathing (sounds, retractions, positioning), and Circulation to the skin (pallor, mottling, cyanosis).

distractorExplanations.b: The ABCs are assessed hands-on in the primary assessment; the triangle is a hands-off visual impression.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulse, blood pressure, and capillary refill require touching the child and are part of the later hands-on assessment.
distractorExplanations.d: Pupils and temperature need hands-on assessment and are not elements of the Pediatric Assessment Triangle.

prompt: You arrive first at a two-car collision on a busy highway. What is your first priority?

options.text: Reach the most seriously injured patient and begin care
Assess scene safety and put on appropriate PPE
Interview witnesses about how the crash happened
Begin triage of all occupants, then notify dispatch

explanation: Scene safety and personal protective equipment come first at every call: traffic, fire, fuel, and unstable vehicles must be recognized and controlled before patient contact. An injured rescuer cannot help anyone and adds to the patient count.

distractorExplanations.a: Rushing to patients before checking traffic, fuel, and other hazards can turn the responder into another casualty.
distractorExplanations.c: Witness accounts may help explain the mechanism later, but they never come before safety or patient care.
distractorExplanations.d: Hazards and resource needs are reported to dispatch early, before committing to triage of individual patients.

prompt: A competent adult refuses transport after your assessment. What should the EMR do?

options.text: Transport anyway under implied consent for safety
Accept a verbal refusal and leave the scene without documenting
Explain risks, ensure understanding, and document refusal
Ask police to place the patient in protective custody

explanation: Informed refusal requires capacity assessment, risk explanation, documentation, and medical control if needed. Leave contact and return instructions per protocol.

distractorExplanations.a: Implied consent applies only to patients who cannot decide; a competent adult has the right to refuse transport.
distractorExplanations.b: Refusals carry high liability; the risks explained, capacity, and the patient's signature must be documented.
distractorExplanations.d: Police custody is for patients who lack capacity or are a danger to themselves; a competent adult may refuse care.

prompt: With whom may you share protected health information (PHI) from a patient care report?

options.text: Family members who call asking about the patient
Reporters at the scene if the patient's name is omitted
Fellow EMTs at other agencies for case review on social media
Receiving facility and personnel involved in patient care

explanation: HIPAA permits sharing PHI without the patient's authorization for treatment, payment, and health care operations. Handing off to the receiving facility and the providers caring for the patient is treatment; anyone else needs authorization or a legal exception.

distractorExplanations.a: Without the patient's permission, family callers are not authorized recipients; HIPAA allows sharing for treatment.
distractorExplanations.b: Other details can still identify a patient; media disclosure requires authorization, not just an omitted name.
distractorExplanations.c: Posting case details publicly breaches PHI even for education; sharing is limited to those involved in care.

prompt: You may come into contact with a patient's blood or body fluids. What do standard precautions require at minimum?

options.text: Gloves and hand hygiene at minimum
Gloves only when the patient appears to be bleeding
Hand sanitizer instead of gloves for fluid contact
N95 respirators and gowns on every call

explanation: Standard precautions treat all blood/body fluids as potentially infectious. Use them whenever contact with blood or body fluids is possible.

distractorExplanations.b: Standard precautions treat all blood and body fluids as potentially infectious, not only visible bleeding.
distractorExplanations.c: Hand hygiene complements but does not replace gloves when contact with body fluids is expected.
distractorExplanations.d: N95s and gowns are transmission-based precautions for specific risks, not the standard-precautions minimum.

prompt: You call dispatch for additional resources at a crash. What information should you provide?

options.text: Patient vital signs and chief complaints for each patient
Location, hazards, number of patients, and resources needed
The mechanism of injury and which driver appears to be at fault
A request made after all patients have been triaged

explanation: Clear concise radio/reporting includes location, problem, hazards, and resource needs. Also state the nature of the incident.

distractorExplanations.a: Detailed vitals belong in the hospital report; a resource request needs location, hazards, patient count, and resources.
distractorExplanations.c: Fault is irrelevant to a resource request; dispatch needs location, hazards, and the number of patients.
distractorExplanations.d: Additional resources are requested early during size-up; waiting until triage ends delays help.

prompt: Which situation most likely requires contacting online medical direction?

options.text: Routine skills already covered by standing orders
Starting CPR on a pulseless adult who has no valid DNR order
Certain medications or protocols outside standing orders
Applying oxygen to a hypoxic patient by protocol

explanation: Online/offline medical control governs extensions beyond standing orders and some refusals. Complex refusals may also need medical direction per local policy.

distractorExplanations.a: Standing orders are offline medical direction; skills they cover need no online contact.
distractorExplanations.b: CPR on a pulseless patient is a standing-order BLS action; it does not wait for online medical direction.
distractorExplanations.d: Oxygen for hypoxia is covered by standing protocols; online direction is for actions beyond them.

prompt: You arrive at a truck crash with a leaking, placarded tanker. As an awareness-level EMR, what should you do?

options.text: Enter the warm zone to begin decontaminating the patients early
Approach from downwind to read the placard up close
Rinse contaminated patients before removing their clothing
Recognize hazard, protect self, and request hazmat specialists

explanation: Awareness-level responders recognize the hazard, stay upwind and uphill at a safe distance, isolate the area and deny entry, and request a hazmat team. Entering contaminated zones or performing decontamination requires higher-level training and PPE.

distractorExplanations.a: Decontamination in the warm zone requires hazmat training and PPE; awareness-level EMRs stay in the cold zone.
distractorExplanations.b: Approach is from upwind and uphill, and placards are read from a safe distance with binoculars.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing clothing removes most contamination first, and decontamination is done by trained hazmat teams.

prompt: Which description fits proper documentation on a patient care report (PCR)?

options.text: Objective, timely, and include assessment findings
Written later from memory once the shift has ended
Corrected by erasing errors so the record looks clean
Focused on your opinion of the patient's behavior

explanation: The PCR is a medical and legal record: complete it promptly with objective findings, interventions, times, and the patient's responses. Errors are corrected with a single line, initials, and date, never erased.

distractorExplanations.b: Delayed documentation loses accuracy and timeliness; the PCR is completed as soon as possible after the call.
distractorExplanations.c: Errors are corrected with a single line, initials, and date; erasing or obliterating looks like falsification.
distractorExplanations.d: Subjective judgments about behavior invite liability; record objective findings and quote the patient.

prompt: In adult START triage, a patient is not breathing and stays apneic after you reposition the airway. How is this patient tagged?

options.text: Immediate/red because airway opening was needed
Expectant/black (deceased or unsalvageable)
Delayed/yellow until rechecked by a paramedic
Immediate/red after five rescue breaths fail

explanation: In START, an adult who does not breathe after the airway is repositioned is tagged expectant (black), so scarce rescuers move on to patients who can be saved. Rescue breaths are not part of adult START; the five-breath step belongs to pediatric JumpSTART.

distractorExplanations.a: Red applies when breathing resumes after airway positioning; apnea that persists after repositioning is expectant/black.
distractorExplanations.c: Delayed is for patients who breathe but cannot walk and lack immediate threats; apneic patients are not held as yellow.
distractorExplanations.d: In JumpSTART, a child still apneic after 5 rescue breaths is tagged expectant, not immediate.

prompt: An adult is found unconscious after a fall and cannot respond. Under what type of consent do you treat?

options.text: Expressed consent from the nearest bystander
Informed consent obtained once the patient wakes
Implied consent for emergency care
Involuntary consent ordered by medical direction

explanation: Implied consent assumes that an unresponsive adult who needs emergency care would agree to it. It applies only while the patient cannot decide and delay would cause harm; once the patient regains capacity, expressed consent is needed.

distractorExplanations.a: Bystanders have no legal authority to consent for an adult; unconscious adults are treated under implied consent.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for the patient to wake could cause harm; emergency care proceeds under implied consent.
distractorExplanations.d: Involuntary consent applies to patients in custody or under court order, not to unconscious adults needing care.

prompt: During a call, an EMR notices injuries on a child that do not match the caregiver's story. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Report only if the child confirms the abuse to you
Confront the caregiver at the scene and ask them to explain the injuries
Document suspicion of abuse as a diagnosis on the PCR
Report per local mandatory reporting laws and ensure child safety

explanation: EMS providers are mandated reporters in most states: reasonable suspicion triggers a report to child protective services or law enforcement per local law. Keep the child safe, document objective findings and exact quotes, and do not accuse anyone on scene.

distractorExplanations.a: Mandatory reporting is triggered by reasonable suspicion; a disclosure or confession is not required.
distractorExplanations.b: Confrontation can escalate danger to the child and crew; document objectively and report to authorities instead.
distractorExplanations.c: The PCR records objective findings and quotes; EMRs do not record abuse as a diagnosis.

prompt: You are dispatched to a reported stabbing, and police are not yet on scene. Where should you stage?

options.text: At a safe distance until law enforcement secures scene
In front of the residence to speed patient access
Close by with emergency lights on so police can locate the unit
Directly behind the first police car as it arrives

explanation: Staging protects crews until scene is safe or escorted by law enforcement. Stage upwind/uphill when hazards are also present.

distractorExplanations.b: Parking at the door exposes the crew; stage out of sight until law enforcement clears the scene.
distractorExplanations.c: Lights and nearby staging draw attention at a violent scene; stage out of sight with lights off.
distractorExplanations.d: Entering with police before the scene is secured places the crew in danger; wait until it is declared safe.

prompt: You are handing a patient over to an arriving ALS crew. What should you do?

options.text: Hand over the patient and send the PCR next week
Provide concise verbal report and complete PCR
Give a full head-to-toe report while ALS treats
Leave once ALS has the patient; ALS documents care

explanation: A handoff is a brief, prioritized verbal report (age, chief complaint, key findings, interventions and responses) followed by a completed patient care report. Every provider documents the care they personally gave, so continuity is not lost.

distractorExplanations.a: The PCR is completed promptly so receiving providers have the record; a delayed report breaks continuity of care.
distractorExplanations.c: Handoff reports are concise and prioritized; long reports during treatment distract the receiving crew.
distractorExplanations.d: Each provider documents their own care; the EMR must still complete a PCR for the care given.

prompt: Which action crosses an ethical boundary for an EMR?

options.text: Reporting a coworker who appears impaired on duty
Honoring a patient's cultural preferences when safe
Accepting a large cash gift from a patient's family
Thanking a family for a homemade card after a call

explanation: A large cash gift creates a conflict of interest and the appearance that care can be bought, so it is declined per agency policy. Small tokens of thanks, respecting cultural preferences, and reporting an impaired colleague are all appropriate conduct.

distractorExplanations.a: Reporting impairment is an ethical duty that protects patients; it does not violate professional boundaries.
distractorExplanations.b: Honoring cultural preferences that do not compromise safety is respectful, patient-centered care, not a boundary violation.
distractorExplanations.d: A small token of thanks with no expectation of favors is generally acceptable; the concern is money that could buy preference.

prompt: Field termination of resuscitation is being considered under protocol and medical direction. Which factor is relevant?

options.text: Patient age over 80 with a long history of heart disease
No shock advised on the first AED analysis
Family request to stop even without a valid DNR
Downtime without ROSC and medical direction criteria

explanation: Termination of resuscitation follows written protocol and medical direction, weighing factors such as prolonged downtime and resuscitation without ROSC. A valid DNR or an unsafe scene are separate reasons to stop or withhold resuscitation.

distractorExplanations.a: Age and comorbidity alone are not termination criteria; protocols use downtime, ROSC, DNR, and medical direction.
distractorExplanations.b: A no-shock message does not mean futility; CPR continues per protocol until termination criteria are met.
distractorExplanations.c: Verbal family wishes without a valid DNR do not meet termination criteria; medical direction decides.

prompt: At a bus crash, you ask everyone who can walk to move to a nearby tree. How are these patients initially tagged in START triage?

options.text: Black (expectant)
Green (minor)
Red (immediate)
Yellow (delayed)

explanation: START first sorts the walking wounded: anyone who can walk to a designated area is tagged green (minor) for now. They are re-triaged later because walking patients can still deteriorate.

distractorExplanations.a: Black is for patients who do not breathe after the airway is repositioned, not for those who can walk.
distractorExplanations.c: Red is for non-ambulatory patients with abnormal respirations, perfusion, or mental status.
distractorExplanations.d: Yellow is for non-ambulatory patients who do not meet red criteria.

prompt: In adult START triage, a non-ambulatory patient is breathing 36 times per minute. Which tag does this patient receive?

options.text: Green (minor)
Yellow (delayed)
Red (immediate)
Black (expectant)

explanation: In START, a non-ambulatory adult breathing more than 30 times per minute is tagged red (immediate) without further checks. Other red triggers are absent radial pulse or capillary refill over 2 seconds, and inability to follow simple commands.

distractorExplanations.a: Green is reserved for patients who can walk; this patient cannot.
distractorExplanations.b: Yellow applies when respirations are 30 or below, perfusion is adequate, and commands are followed.
distractorExplanations.d: Black applies when the patient does not breathe even after the airway is repositioned.

prompt: A non-ambulatory adult at a mass casualty incident is breathing 22 times per minute, has a strong radial pulse, and follows simple commands. Which START category applies?

options.text: Green (minor)
Red (immediate)
Black (expectant)
Yellow (delayed)

explanation: A patient who cannot walk but breathes 30 or fewer times per minute, has a radial pulse (or capillary refill of 2 seconds or less), and follows commands is tagged yellow (delayed) in START.

distractorExplanations.a: Green is only for patients who can walk; a non-ambulatory patient cannot be tagged minor.
distractorExplanations.b: Red requires a red trigger: respirations over 30, poor perfusion, or failure to follow commands.
distractorExplanations.c: Black is for patients who remain apneic after airway repositioning.

prompt: You are the first EMS unit at a multi-vehicle crash with many patients. Under NIMS, what is one of your first responsibilities?

options.text: Establish command and give a size-up report
Begin treating the first patient you reach
Wait for a supervisor before reporting
Transport the most critical patient yourself

explanation: Under the National Incident Management System, the first arriving unit establishes incident command, gives a size-up report with the number of patients and hazards, requests resources, and begins triage. Command transfers as senior personnel arrive.

distractorExplanations.b: Committing to one patient leaves the scene uncoordinated; the first unit organizes resources first.
distractorExplanations.c: Command is established by the first arriving unit; waiting delays the request for more resources.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving with one patient abandons the incident before command, triage, and resources are in place.

prompt: An overturned tanker shows a placard with a four-digit UN number. Which reference identifies the material and the initial isolation distance?

options.text: The receiving hospital's safety data sheets
The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG)
The vehicle's registration and insurance card
The local EMS patient treatment protocol

explanation: The DOT Emergency Response Guidebook links the four-digit UN/NA number on a placard to a guide page with hazards, protective actions, and initial isolation and evacuation distances. Read placards from a distance with binoculars.

distractorExplanations.a: Safety data sheets describe chemicals at a workplace; they are not the roadside tool for placarded shipments.
distractorExplanations.c: Registration papers identify the vehicle owner, not the hazardous cargo or isolation distance.
distractorExplanations.d: Treatment protocols guide patient care; they do not identify hazardous materials by UN number.

prompt: You and a partner are lifting a loaded stretcher. Which technique best protects your back?

options.text: Bend at the waist with straight legs and lift quickly
Twist toward the vehicle as you lift the stretcher
Power lift with feet apart, back locked, and legs lifting
Hold the stretcher at arm's length, well away from your body

explanation: The power lift uses feet shoulder-width apart, a locked (straight) back, and the legs to lift, with the load close to the body. Communicate with your partner and avoid twisting; pivot with the feet instead.

distractorExplanations.a: Bending at the waist with straight legs places the load on the lower back and causes injury.
distractorExplanations.b: Twisting while lifting is a leading cause of back injury; turn with your feet after the lift.
distractorExplanations.d: Holding the load away from the body multiplies the strain on the back; keep it close.

prompt: A patient with possible spinal injury is trapped in a car that has caught fire. What is appropriate?

options.text: Apply a cervical collar and short spine board before moving
Wait for fire suppression before moving him
Lift him out by the arms and legs quickly
Use an emergency move such as a long-axis drag

explanation: When there is immediate danger such as fire, an emergency move is made before full immobilization. A long-axis drag (by clothing, shoulders, or blanket) pulls along the length of the body to limit spinal movement.

distractorExplanations.a: Full immobilization takes minutes the patient does not have in a burning vehicle; immediate danger comes first.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for suppression may expose the patient to fatal burns or smoke; move him if it is safe for you.
distractorExplanations.c: Lifting by the limbs bends and twists the spine; a long-axis drag keeps it as aligned as possible.

prompt: A patient sues an EMR for negligence. Which elements must generally be proven?

options.text: Duty, breach of duty, damages, and causation
Duty, consent, abandonment, and damages
Intent, breach of duty, and malice
A breach of duty and a poor patient outcome, nothing more

explanation: Negligence requires four elements: a duty to act, a breach of that duty (failure to meet the standard of care), damages (actual harm), and proximate causation (the breach caused the harm).

distractorExplanations.b: Consent and abandonment are separate legal issues; they are not the four elements of negligence.
distractorExplanations.c: Intent and malice relate to intentional torts such as assault, not negligence, which is unintentional.
distractorExplanations.d: A poor outcome alone is not negligence; duty and causation must also be proven.

prompt: An EMR leaves a stable patient with a bystander to answer another call before the ambulance arrives. Which legal issue does this create?

options.text: Assault, by threatening the patient with harm
Abandonment of a patient who still needs care
Battery, by touching the patient without consent
Libel, by making false written statements

explanation: Abandonment is ending care of a patient who still needs it without handing over to a provider of equal or higher training. A bystander does not qualify, so care must continue until a qualified provider takes over.

distractorExplanations.a: Assault is placing a person in fear of bodily harm, not leaving the patient's care.
distractorExplanations.c: Battery is touching a patient without consent, not ending care prematurely.
distractorExplanations.d: Libel is a false written statement that damages a person's reputation.

prompt: A hospice patient in cardiac arrest has a valid, signed DNR order presented by the family. What should the EMR do?

options.text: Start CPR until a physician arrives
Start CPR because the family is upset
Withhold CPR and provide comfort and support
Give rescue breaths without compressions until ALS arrives

explanation: A valid DNR order (form requirements vary by state) directs that CPR not be started. Verify it per protocol, withhold resuscitation, provide comfort and emotional support to the family, and contact medical direction if there is doubt.

distractorExplanations.a: A valid DNR is a physician order; waiting for a physician on scene is not required to honor it.
distractorExplanations.b: Family distress does not override a valid DNR; support the family while honoring the order.
distractorExplanations.d: Rescue breathing is resuscitation; a DNR order in cardiac arrest means no resuscitation attempts.

prompt: An off-duty EMR stops at a crash and provides care in good faith within her training. What generally provides legal protection in most states?

options.text: The implied consent doctrine
Standing orders
The duty to act
Good Samaritan laws

explanation: Good Samaritan laws in most states protect people who help in an emergency in good faith, without compensation, and within their training. They vary by state and do not protect against gross negligence.

distractorExplanations.a: Implied consent permits treatment of an unresponsive patient; it does not protect the rescuer from liability.
distractorExplanations.b: Standing orders authorize care within an EMS system; they do not protect off-duty volunteers.
distractorExplanations.c: The duty to act creates an obligation; it is a basis for liability, not protection from it.

prompt: Medical direction gives you a treatment order by radio. What should you do before acting on it?

options.text: Repeat the order back word for word and confirm it
Act immediately without repeating it to save time
Use ten-codes so the order stays private
Ask the patient whether to follow the order

explanation: Repeat the order back exactly (echo technique) and wait for confirmation before acting. If an order seems unclear or inappropriate, ask for clarification. Document the order, the physician, and the time.

distractorExplanations.b: Skipping the repeat-back risks acting on a misheard order; confirmation takes seconds.
distractorExplanations.c: Ten-codes vary between agencies and cause misunderstanding; plain language is preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: The patient may consent or refuse, but confirming the order itself is done with medical direction.

prompt: Police have restrained a violently agitated patient for transport. How should the patient be positioned?

options.text: Face down with the wrists tied to the ankles
Supine or on the side with breathing monitored
Face down with a responder's weight on the back
Sitting with a towel tied over the face

explanation: Restrained patients are positioned supine or on their side, never prone or hog-tied, because those positions cause positional asphyxia. Monitor airway, breathing, and circulation continuously, and check distal circulation in restrained limbs.

distractorExplanations.a: Prone hog-tie restraint impairs breathing and is linked to positional asphyxia and death.
distractorExplanations.c: Weight on the back of a prone patient restricts chest expansion and causes asphyxia.
distractorExplanations.d: Covering the face blocks the airway; a spit hood or surgical mask is used per protocol instead.

prompt: You are stuck by a used needle while cleaning up after a call. What should you do first?

options.text: Squeeze the wound to bleed it, then report it at shift end
Apply bleach to the wound and finish the call
Wash the site with soap and water and report it now
Report it only if the patient is known infected

explanation: After a needlestick, immediately wash the site with soap and water, then report the exposure to your supervisor or designated infection control officer at once so post-exposure evaluation and prophylaxis can begin promptly.

distractorExplanations.a: Delaying the report delays post-exposure testing and treatment, which work best within hours.
distractorExplanations.b: Bleach and caustic agents damage skin and are not recommended for wound care after exposure.
distractorExplanations.d: Every exposure is reported because a patient's infection status is often unknown.

prompt: A patient with fever, night sweats, and a persistent bloody cough may have tuberculosis. Which PPE is appropriate?

options.text: A surgical mask for you and a fit-tested N95 respirator on the patient
Gloves alone, because TB spreads by touch
A gown and gloves, because TB spreads by contact
A fit-tested N95 for you and a surgical mask on the patient

explanation: Tuberculosis requires airborne precautions: the responder wears a fit-tested N95 respirator, and the patient wears a surgical mask if tolerated (or oxygen by nonrebreather if needed). Improve ventilation in the vehicle.

distractorExplanations.a: A surgical mask does not protect the wearer from airborne droplet nuclei, and an N95 on the patient is uncomfortable and unnecessary.
distractorExplanations.b: TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, so gloves alone do not protect the responder.
distractorExplanations.c: Contact precautions do not stop airborne transmission; respiratory protection is required.
